name: Archival Experimental Editorial
description: 1:1 minimalist experimental editorial collage combining a monochrome photographic subject, archival data graphics, a scientific circular diagram, tinted paper, and one dynamically controlled geometric highlight.
systemPrompt:
Create a fixed 1:1 square minimalist experimental editorial collage using {{subjectImage}} as the primary and only content reference. Preserve the subject's identity, appearance, physical structure, pose, silhouette, clothing, proportions, geometry, orientation, and recognizable characteristics with high fidelity. Do not invent, replace, redesign, or significantly distort the subject.

Transform the subject into a monochrome black-and-white photographic reproduction with rich matte blacks, controlled dark-gray shadows, soft gray midtones, paper-influenced highlights, believable source lighting, and restrained photographic contrast. Keep the subject immediately recognizable and visually dominant, occupying approximately 60–75% of the square canvas with a close or medium-close crop and an intentionally offset editorial placement. Maintain generous negative space.

Use {{backgroundColor}} as the base archival paper color while preserving aged physical-paper qualities such as subtle fibers, speckles, stains, unevenness, photocopy contamination, and restrained print imperfections. Keep the background minimal and free of detailed environments.

Place one large, delicate thin-line circular technical diagram behind the subject. It should behave like a conceptual halo or analytical instrument, extend beyond the subject on multiple sides, and remain partially obscured by the subject. Build it from concentric circles, radial divisions, measurement ticks, scientific plotting structures, navigational geometry, engineering notation, statistical-wheel forms, fragmentary notes, tiny index numbers, and technical symbols. Keep it archival and imperfect rather than digitally precise.

Include one substantial archival-data graphic region tinted {{overlayTintColor}}. It should intersect or overlap the subject and feel physically screen-printed, photocopied, offset-printed, or overprinted. Fill it with dense black archival information such as plotting curves, grids, numeric columns, financial traces, measurements, coordinates, technical labels, document fragments, ruled grids, tabulated values, handwritten annotations, index numbers, symbols, and small diagrammatic marks. Keep this information fragmented and primarily visual rather than forming prominent readable typography.

Add exactly one primary graphic highlight element controlled by {{highlightShape}} and rendered entirely in {{highlightColor}}. Interpret {{highlightShape}} literally and reproduce the requested geometry. If it describes a horizontal, vertical, or diagonal strip, create a bold archival strip with consistent visual thickness and allow it to intersect, pass across, pass behind, or partially overlap the subject. If it describes a non-strip shape such as a circle, semicircle, square, triangle, oval, diamond, polygon, trapezoid, crescent, arc, irregular block, or another geometry, generate that exact shape and dynamically anchor it to a suitable edge of the subject's visible silhouette. Its placement may vary between generations across meaningful structural regions such as the head, shoulder, torso, arm, hand, leg, product perimeter, sculpture contour, or architectural edge. Keep the placement intentionally composed, partially overlapping the subject where appropriate, and never floating randomly in empty space. Avoid obscuring defining facial or structural features.

Render {{highlightColor}} as physical printed pigment, offset ink, photocopy toner, or analog registration ink. Do not turn it into neon lighting, glowing CGI, transparent glass, digital lens flare, holographic UI, or a modern gradient. Allow subtle ink irregularity, print grain, and imperfect pigment coverage.

Maintain a clear visual hierarchy: recognizable monochrome subject first, {{highlightShape}} in {{highlightColor}} second, archival-data region in {{overlayTintColor}} third, technical circular diagram fourth, and archival paper in {{backgroundColor}} fifth. Use only deep black, grayscale photographic tones, {{backgroundColor}}, {{overlayTintColor}}, and {{highlightColor}}. Do not introduce arbitrary accent colors.

The aesthetic should combine late-20th-century experimental editorial design, 1960s–1980s avant-garde magazine graphics, Japanese experimental publication design, restrained Swiss modernism, constructivist photomontage, scientific and financial archival documents, vintage photocopy reproduction, and offset-printed academic material. The subject must remain fundamentally photographic rather than becoming a painting, vector illustration, cartoon, comic, 3D render, or digital artwork.

Apply controlled analog imperfections including fine photographic grain, halftone dots, photocopy noise, dry toner texture, rough ink edges, subtle paper grain, faint offset-print misregistration, irregular ink density, distressed technical linework, faded marks, and microscopic printing flaws. Keep the result sophisticated, cerebral, analytical, archival, slightly dystopian, and deliberately imperfect without excessive distress.

Do not add extra people, limbs, products, unrelated objects, branding, logos, prominent headlines, slogans, captions, modern UI elements, stickers, badges, arrows, decorative icons, modern infographics, futuristic holographic interfaces, glossy gradients, neon effects, 3D typography, painterly brushwork, anime, comic, cartoon, vector-art, digital-painting aesthetics, detailed photographic environments, or arbitrary accent colors. Do not alter the subject's identity, anatomy, facial structure, hairstyle, expression, clothing, accessories, or recognizable object geometry. Do not ignore {{highlightShape}}, change {{highlightColor}}, change {{backgroundColor}}, or repeatedly place the highlight on the same subject region. Do not let the highlight completely obscure the subject. Do not make the technical diagram digitally perfect or the archival data perfectly legible. Do not fill all negative space. The final result must look like a deliberately composed analog editorial artifact rather than a contemporary digital template with a vintage filter applied afterward.
